R E S E A R C H A R T I C L E - M E T H O D O L O G Y
# CoBRA without experts: New paradigm for software development effort estimation using COCOMO metrics

Elham Feizpour [1] | Hooman Tahayori [1] | Ashkan Sami [1,2]


1 Department of Computer Science and

Engineering and IT, School of Electrical and

Computer Engineering, Shiraz University,

Shiraz, Iran

2 Edinburgh Napier University, Edinburgh, UK

Correspondence

Hooman Tahayori, Department of Computer

Electrical and Computer Engineering, Shiraz

University, Shiraz, Iran.

[Email: tahayori@shirazu.ac.ir](mailto:tahayori@shirazu.ac.ir)

1 | INTRODUCTION


Abstract

Software development effort estimation (SDEE) is a critical activity in developing

software. Accurate effort estimation in the early phases of software design life cycle

has important effects on the success of software projects. COCOMO (Constructive

Cost Model) is a parametric data-driven SDEE model whose parameters must be cali
brated with an organization's local data for accurate estimation. Such data are scarce

for most organizations. On the other hand, CoBRA (Cost estimation, Benchmarking,

and Risk Assessment) is one of the powerful hybrid methods that need a small num
ber of local historical data for effort estimation. However, data gathering in CoBRA is

time-consuming and costly. To ease the use of CoBRA, in this paper, we design a

methodology that extracts CoBRA-required data from COCOMO datasets. By the

proposed method, data collected for COCOMO would be used in CoBRA. Using

CoBRA, a more accurate estimation of the required effort would be achieved with

fewer number of historical data than what is required to calibrate the COCOMO

model. We apply the proposed method on six well-known public COCOMO datasets

and use them in CoBRA. Obtained results depict an increase in the accuracy of esti
mations in comparison with other existing methods.

K E Y W O R D S

CoBRA, COCOMO, cost driver, effort multiplier, software development effort estimation


There are two major software development methodologies, classical waterfall-based and agile. [1,2] In waterfall-style development, each phase of the

software development starts only when the prior phase is completed. Moreover, the final software product will be delivered after the last phase

is fulfilled. Planning, designing, and testing phases in agile development, however, are iterative and incremental, and a new version of the product

is developed in each iteration. Agile development process that uses continuous integrations of small codes to produce the final software does not

require a strict estimation of the overall required effort. Instead, they need short-term estimations of the effort required to do the current task. [1]

Waterfall methodology is still the most appropriate software development methodology for large-scale projects and is mainly used in large

governmental or military projects and also for projects whose budgets must be known in advance. [1] Estimating the required effort in waterfall
style projects is an important issue because due to the size of such projects and their vitality, overestimation or underestimation of the required

effort may drastically affect the projects and the software development companies.

Software development effort estimation (SDEE) as one of the main concerns for software project managers [3] is defined as “the process of

predicting the effort required to develop a software system.” [4] SDEE in waterfall projects enables determining the right budget before starting the

work. [1] Poor estimation is one of the most common causes of software project failures. [5] On one hand, overestimation of the efforts leads a com
pany to allocate extra budget and human resources for the project that wastes the company's resources and causes loss of customers because of

J Softw Evol Proc. 2023;35:e2569. [wileyonlinelibrary.com/journal/smr](http://wileyonlinelibrary.com/journal/smr) © 2023 John Wiley & Sons Ltd. 1 of 32

[https://doi.org/10.1002/smr.2569](https://doi.org/10.1002/smr.2569)

|2 of 32|FEIZPOUR ET AL.|
|---|---|
|||


extra bid for the project. On the other hand, underestimation can lead to a lower quality product or even project failure. Appropriate SDEE

method helps project managers to have better control on the project and complete the project on time and within the budget.

COCOMO and CoBRA [6,7] are two SDEE methods that can be used for waterfall-style projects. COCOMO [8] and its newer version, COCOMO
               II, [9] are parametric data driven models that are built from past completed project data (historical data). Menzies et al. have recommended that

COCOMO must be used while COCOMO-style datasets are available [10] and the parameters of COCOMO must be calibrated for specific organiza
tion and context. Calibration process in COCOMO is difficult and requires dozens of historical data. AS is discussed in Nguyen et al., [5] at least

10 historical data are needed to calibrate two main coefficients of the COCOMO-II model. In the real world, not enough historical data in a new

context or in a newly established software organization exist.

To adjust the parameters of these methods toward improving their accuracy, recent studies have exploited meta-heuristic algorithms. Notably,

Kumari and Pushkar [11] have used a hybrid Cuckoo and Harmony algorithm, whereas Fadhil et al. [12] have utilized the Dolphin algorithm to optimize

the estimation of COCOMO models. Nguyen et al. [5] have proposed a calibrating method for COCOMO using small windows of the most recently

completed projects. Some studies [13,14] have used fuzzy technique to handle uncertainty and vagueness in the parameters of the COCOMO model.

Recently, researchers have integrated optimization algorithms like genetic algorithm (GA) [15] and particle swarm optimization (PSO) [16] to optimize

the parameters of fuzzy model-based COCOMO. In Singh et al., [17] artificial neural network (ANN) is integrated with COCOMO.

CoBRA introduced by Briand et al. [6,7] is a hybrid method that uses experts' knowledge and historical data simultaneously. It can be

implemented with small datasets and does not require any calibration. CoBRA balances the need of historical data and experts' knowledge in the

estimation process. Achieving high estimation accuracy with minimal data requirements and generating reusable cost model across similar projects

can be counted as the strengths of CoBRA. [7] It is notable that collecting data to be used in CoBRA is time-consuming and requires expertise and

training. There are few effort estimation researches on this method. [6,18][–][20] Moreover, because of the confidentiality reasons, data and some

results of these research are not publicly available. To the best of our knowledge, there is no public dataset to meet the data requirements of the

CoBRA method and its efficiency and effectiveness are not compared with other SDEE methods.

In this study, we propose a mapping algorithm to generate CoBRA required data from the datasets collected for COCOMO and

COCOMO-II models. More precisely, with the proposed mapping algorithm, we transform the COCOMO and COCOMO-II existing datasets

to meet the CoBRA requirements. The importance of this transformation lies in the fact that collecting data for methods like COCOMO is

straightforward and well established but data collection for CoBRA is difficult and time-consuming. However, as we will show, when there

is no enough local historical data in a specific organization to calibrate the parameters of the COCOMO model, CoBRA can more accurately

estimate the required effort.

We apply the proposed transformation method on open-source COCOMO-style datasets that are collected to be used with COCOMO and

COCOMO-II. Hence, initially, we make them applicable in CoBRA. Then, we compare estimations obtained by CoBRA with some well-known

SDEE methods, using the same datasets. Obtained results on the COCOMO-style datasets show that CoBRA with a small number of historical

projects can better predict efforts than other existing methods. Moreover, the generated datasets in this study could be used in future CoBRA

research.

In summary, the questions that this research tries to answer are as follows:

� RQ1: Considering the similarity of the nature of the COCOMO and CoBRA, is it possible (how) to provide a method to generate CoBRA
required data from the datasets collected for COCOMO?

� RQ2: How is the effectiveness of the CoBRA method compared to other effort estimation methods?

� RQ3: At least with how many historical projects CoBRA can predict the software effort accurately?

� RQ4: Can CoBRA be a good alternative for COCOMO when there is insufficient historical data to calibrate COCOMO?

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, related research on SDEE are reviewed. A fast review on the CoBRA method and

COCOMO model is provided in Section 3. In Section 4, our proposed transformation method for adjusting datasets to be applicable in CoBRA is

explained. The experimental design is explained in Section 5. In Section 6, obtained results on the datasets and also the results of statistical analy
sis on the conducted experiments are presented. In Section 7, performance of the proposed method on different datasets is compared with other

methods. Section 8 discusses the major threats to the validity of the study. Finally, Section 9 concludes the paper.

2 | RELATED RESEARCH

Different SDEE methods and techniques are developed in recent years, but getting more accurate and reliable predictions is still a challenging

problem. Some extensive reviews have investigated the existing methods for SDEE from different perspectives. [4,21][–][23] SDEE methods can be

broadly categorized into experts' judgments, data-driven methods, and hybrid methods. [24]

|FEIZPOUR ET AL.|3 of 32|
|---|---|
|||


The first approach that is introduced for SDEE relies on experts' judgments. [23] In expert-driven approaches, [25,26] several experienced experts

familiar with the context of software provide independent estimations, and then consensus methods are used to get the final effort estimation. In

the absence of sufficient historical data, expert-based methods can be used in SDEE, but these methods are expensive and may suffer from incon
sistent, biased, and limited access to experts. [27] Moreover, such methods are not easily repeatable. [6]

The second category of SDEE consists of data-driven methods. The accuracy of these methods completely depends on the quantity and qual
ity of the data used to construct the model. These methods usually require large sets of high-quality historical projects. Data gathering in software

engineering is time-consuming and difficult. Furthermore, the value of collected data may decrease over time because of the advancements in

technology or changes within the company. [28] Most of the software production companies do not have sufficient and well-documented past pro
ject data to systematically build such effort estimation models. One of the main categories of data-driven models are algorithmic models including

COCOMO, [8] COCOMO II, [9] SLIM, [29] and Function Point Analysis. [30] Parameters of these models must be calibrated with local historical data that is

usually scarce in companies.

A wide range of data mining techniques are used for SDEE. A comparative study of these methods is presented in Dejaeger et al. [23] These

methods include various regression techniques such as ordinary least squares (OLS) regression, [31] robust regression (RoR), [32] ridge regression

(RiR), [23] support vector regression (SVR), [3] multiple linear regression (MLR), stepwise regression (SWR), and classification and regression tree

(CART). These methods are wildly used in different researches, for example. [1,23,33,34]

Different types of ANN such as multi-layered perceptron (MLP) [35] and radial basis function (RBF) [23,36] are also utilized in SDEE. Recently, a

number of researches have integrated ANN with the other SDEE methods to improve the accuracy of their estimations. [11,37,38]

Analogy-based software effort estimation (ABE) is another widely used method in SDEE. [39] ABE methods are based on the assumption

that the projects of similar characteristics require similar efforts. [40][–][43] Hence, they focus on finding the former completed projects that are

most similar to the target project. Then, taking the actual effort of such completed projects, they predict the required effort for the target

project. The accuracy of ABE is not satisfactory, so many studies have tried to increase its accuracy by integrating it with different

methods. Combination of ABE and PSO, [44] ABE and ANN, [45] and ABE and differential evolution-based model [46] are other types of the

ABE method. In order to achieve a high-performance model, some studies have combined several estimation methods using specific

selection methods or combination rules to estimate the effort. [1,33,47][–][50] Jose Thiago and Oliveira [50] have introduced a dynamic ensemble

selection method of 15 regression models to obtain better accuracy in the predictions. Many of the new methods that are introduced in

recent studies are complicated and are not practical in the real world because they require many past project data and special skills and

knowledge.

The third category of SDEE methods consists of hybrid methods that use combination of experts' knowledge and historical data to estimate

software development effort. Examples of these methods are CoBRA [6,7] and Bayesian belief network. [51][–][53] CoBRA is a method with high predictive

power, high flexibility, and reusability with minimal data requirements. [24] But this method is rather ignored in recent studies. Collecting data to be

used in CoBRA is time-consuming and difficult, which can be a reason for CoBRA to be overlooked.

Few studies have used the CoBRA method to estimate software development effort. [6,18][–][20,54][–][56] Table 1 shows a few former projects that

have relied on CoBRA for estimating their required efforts. In Ruhe et al., [18] CoBRA is used for estimating the effort of 12 web applications of a

small Australian company, and its result shows the mean magnitude of relative error (MMRE) of 0.17. In Trendowicz et al., [19] CoBRA is used in the

iterative manner for Oki Electric Industry in Japan, and the achieved MMRE has been 0.12, and PRED (0.25) of 100% means that all predictions

were within 25% of the actual values. These results are very significant and satisfactory. CoBRA is also used in Nakaoa et al. [20] to estimate the

effort of independent verification and validation of mission-critical software systems. The results of this research proved that CoBRA can provide

more reliable estimates than expert-base estimation and OLS models.

TABLE 1 Approximate costs of the applying CoBRA method on some case study.

3 | BACKGROUND

In this section, we provide a brief introduction to COCOMO and CoBRA methods and present the required definitions.

3.1 | COCOMO

The Constructive Cost Model (COCOMO), proposed by Boehem, [8] is a data-driven and algorithmic estimation model that defines mathematical

relations for estimating the effort required to develop a software project. COCOMO has three variants, namely, basic, intermediate, and detailed.

Basic COCOMO, suitable for quick and early estimations of software effort, has limited accuracy because it only provides a regression model based

on the lines of code (size) and does not consider other attributes. Intermediate COCOMO considers some characteristics of projects that affect

their efforts. Such characteristics that make the projects with the same size to demand for different efforts are referred to as “cost drivers.”

Detailed COCOMO, however, is used when the software life-cycle architecture has been developed. Detailed COCOMO in addition to cost drivers,

accounts the effects of each phase of the project on the required effort.

In intermediate COCOMO [8] model, the required effort is calculated as

where Effort represents the needed development effort for a project in person/months. Size is thousands of lines of delivered source code

(KLOC). A and B, however, are two factors that can be calibrated depending on the characteristics of the software development company to

reflect the local development environment. [23] EM i depicts the i [th] effort multiplier (EM) that is a numeric value associated with the rating level of

i [th] cost driver. The rating level of a cost driver has a qualitative value that expresses the impact of the cost driver on the development effort.

These rating levels range from “very low” to “extra high.” EM i s are calculated via regression on historical data. [23]

In COCOMO, three modes of software are identified: Organic, Semi-detached, and Embedded. The values of A and B in the three modes are

shown in Table 2.

Table 3 represents the cost drivers and associated EMs used in the intermediate COCOMO.

Cost driver with nominal rating level always has an EM equal to 1.0 (see Table 3, column “N”), which means that it does not

change the overall development effort. If a rating level indicates an increase of the software development effort, then its corresponding EM

would be more than 1.0. Conversely, if the rating level indicates a reduction of the development effort, then the corresponding EM is

less than 1.0. When all cost drivers are set to nominal rating level, the calculated efforts—that would be (A � Size [B] )—is referred to as the

nominal effort.

COCOMO-II, [9] introduced in 2000 as the enhanced version of COCOMO, [9] is created by analyzing 161 projects from different organizations.

However, the data based on which this model is developed are not publicly available. In this version, five new attributes called scale factors that

have an exponential impact on the effort are introduced. Also, 17 cost drivers are defined, and EMs are updated. Effort in COCOMO-II is calcu
lated as

3.2 | CoBRA method

The CoBRA (Cost estimation, Benchmarking, and Risk Assessment) method was introduced in 1998 and first used in German companies. [6] To esti
mate the effort of a new project, CoBRA needs the project size, the characteristics that affect the effort of the project, and the extent of their

affect based on expert judgment as well as the information of several similar completed projects—Figure 1A. Software effort estimation in CoBRA

is based on the idea that a project effort consists of two basic components: nominal effort and effort overhead. More precisely, [7]

Effort ¼ Effort Nom þ EOð � Effort Nom Þ ð3Þ

where Effort is the effort required to develop a software project. Nominal effort Effortð Nom ) depicts the required effort for developing the project

under the optimum conditions in a specific context. The project that is developed under such optimal conditions is called nominal project. EO is

Effort Overhead and refers to the additional effort required to overcome shortcomings of a real project environment, such as insufficient skills of

the project team and high complexity of software. In effect, EO represents the percentage increase of effort in a real project relative to the nomi
nal project. [20] Figure 1 schematically shows how effort is calculated with CoBRA.

In order to estimate the software development effort, CoBRA uses two components: effort overhead model and productivity model. Effort over
head model (or causal model) in a certain context consists of factors influencing the effort overhead and their inter-relationships. These factors are

called effort drivers that are determined by a questionnaire [6] or through interviewing domain experts and project managers. [18] Each effort driver

has either Positive or Negative relationship with the effort—arrows labeled “+” and arrows labeled “�” in Figure 1B, respectively. Effort drivers

with positive relationship increase the effort overhead as their value increases. However, an effort driver with a negative relationship increases

the effort overhead as its value decreases. There are two types of relationships: direct and indirect. A direct relationship (solid arrow in Figure 1B)

means that the effort driver directly increases effort overhead regardless of the values of the other effort drivers. An indirect relationship (dashed

arrow in Figure 1B) indicates an interaction effect and indicates how the effort driver affects other effort drivers.

Similar to COCOMO, each effort driver has qualitative and quantitative values that indicate its impact rate on the effort. The quantified

impact of an effort driver on software effort is also called effort multiplier (EM)—similar to COCOMO. The value of each EM indicates the percent
age of additional effort for completing the project compared to the nominal project. For example, if EM for an effort driver with “high” qualitative

value is 20%, then the project requires 120% of the nominal effort. In CoBRA, the value of an EM is elicited from experts. In order to handle

FIGURE 1 Components of CoBRA model 26.

|FEIZPOUR ET AL.|7 of 32|
|---|---|
|||


experts' uncertainty, each expert can use either of the three EM values for each effort driver: minimum, most likely, and maximum. These values

depict the percentage of the increase in effort caused by the effort drivers and are modeled by triangular distributions. With the Monte Carlo

simulation, [56] sampling is performed on each of these distributions and each sample value is used to obtain an effort overhead estimate. This pro
cess is repeated many times, and finally, the distribution of effort for a project would be obtained—Figure 1D.

Productivity model determines the relationship between actual effort and the size and effort overhead of projects in a specific context. It is

used to determine nominal productivity (P Nom ) that refers to the development productivity of a nominal project. [7] To determine P Nom, data from

some similar historical projects are used in order to identify a relationship between effort overhead and actual project effort. In CoBRA, nominal

productivity is assumed to have constant value across projects in the same context, that is, nominal productivity can be assumed the same for sim
ilar projects. It is used as a baseline for estimating efforts of new projects. [6,7] Theoretically, nominal productivity for each historical project

i (P Nom ið Þ) can be determined. If the right side of Equation (3) is multiplied and divided by the size of project, according to classical definition of

productivity in software engineering (productivity ¼ effort [size] [),] [57] [ effort would be]

1
EFfort ¼ � size � ð1 þ EOÞ ð4Þ
P Nom

So, nominal productivity for each historical project i can be determined by

P Nom ið Þ ¼ [1] [þ] [EO] [i] ð5Þ
Effort act i

where EO i is the effort overhead of project i, size is the size of the project i in KLOC, and Effort act i is the actual effort for developing the project i.

To determine a crisp-value baseline nominal productivity (P Nom ), a median approach [18] or regression analysis [7] is usually used. In the median

approach, first, the nominal productivity for each historical project using its effort overhead and size and actual effort using Equation (5) is calcu
lated. Next, the median of the nominal productivities is obtained as P Nom . In the regression approach, the inverse of the slope of the best-fit

regression line f : Size � ð1þ EOÞ ! Effort across the historical projects is used as P Nom —Figure 1C. Trendowicz [7] has mentioned that “the nominal

productivity regression line represents a simple bivariate relationship that does not require a large dataset. This is important, as it explains why

CoBRA does not have demanding data requirements, as opposed to data-driven estimation techniques.”

4 | PROPOSED METHOD

In this section, we discuss the proposed method that enables a software company that does not have adequate historical data in COCOMO for
mat, to use CoBRA and achieve higher accuracy of effort estimation.

To show the effectiveness of the proposed method, we have used some public datasets that are developed to be used in COCOMO. In these

datasets, each project is described with COCOMO cost drivers and their linguistic values and numeric values for size and effort. The proposed

method converts the data collected for COCOMO into the data required by CoBRA and extracts the components of the CoBRA, including the

effort overhead model, EMs, and productivity model. In the following, we illustrate in detail the extraction of CoBRA components from COCOMO

data. The proposed method can be similarly applied on the datasets collected for COCOMO-II.

4.1 | COCOMO cost drivers versus CoBRA effort drivers

To obtain effort overhead model in CoBRA, factors that affect software effort must be determined. In CoBRA, these factors should be identified

and ranked by experts in several brainstorming sessions, which is a difficult step to be fulfilled. However, because identifying cost drivers in

COCOMO is more established, in this section, we demonstrate a methodology for deriving CoBRA effort drivers based on the COCOMO cost

drivers.

Cost drivers in COCOMO are divided into three groups [58] :

- Cost drivers that increase in their rating level increase the project effort. They are known as positive-influencing cost drivers.

- Cost drivers that increase in their rating level reduce the project effort. These cost drivers are referred to as negative-influencing cost drivers.

- “sced” cost driver that defines project's schedule-related constraint.

|8 of 32|FEIZPOUR ET AL.|
|---|---|
|||


Positive-influencing cost drivers in COCOMO are stor, data, time, turn, virt, cplx, and rely. For example, as is shown in Table 3, “High” (H) rating

of cplx—product complexity—will add 15% to the estimated effort. When its rating level increases to “Very High” (VH) or “Extra High” (XH), extra

30% or 65% effort would be required, respectively. We consider positive-influencing cost drivers in COCOMO as positive relationship effort

drivers in CoBRA.

Negative-influencing cost drivers in COCOMO are acap, pcap, aexp, modp, tool, vexp, and lexp. For example, with respect to Table 3, “High”

(H) rating of acap—analyst capability—will reduce 14% (its EM is 0.86) of the project effort and “Very High” (VH) acap rating will reduce 29% (its

EM is 0.71).

“sced” cost driver in COCOMO is a special cost driver. As can be seen in Table 3, by increasing the rating level of “sced,” effort does not reg
ularly increase or regularly decrease. So, depending on the value of rating level, it can be put in both positive-influencing cost drivers group and

negative-influencing cost drivers group.

Figure 2 shows how COCOMO cost drivers can be viewed in the CoBRA effort overhead model. As can be seen in the figure, this EO model

depicts only the direct relationship between each effort driver and the effort overhead. This is due to the fact that the cost drivers in COCOMO

are orthogonal [8] and do not have interaction with each other.

4.2 | Calculating CoBRA EMs from COCOMO model

The concept of nominal rating level differs in COCOMO and CoBRA. In COCOMO, nominal rating level refers to ordinary or normal conditions

and its assigned EM is 1. More precisely, if a cost driver is evaluated as nominal (normal), no reduction or extra effort would be imposed by that

cost driver. However, in CoBRA, the nominal rating level for an effort driver refers to the ideal state of that effort driver. In other words, in

CoBRA, an effort driver that is evaluated as nominal indicates that the effort driver would not cause an effort overhead. So, according to the nom
inal concept in these two methods, it can be inferred that the rating level of cost driver of the COCOMO with the minimum EM value corresponds

to the ideal state of the CoBRA method, that is, the CoBRA nominal state, and thus, its CoBRA EM value should be set to zero. In order to calcu
late other EMs corresponding to each rating level of CoBRA effort drivers, we calculate the difference between the COCOMO EM value

corresponding to that rating level and the COCOMO EM value designated as the CoBRA nominal state.

For calculating CoBRA EM from positive-influencing COCOMO cost drivers group, the ideal state of a cost driver is its lowest rating level that

does not cause any effort overhead in CoBRA. For example, “cplx” cost driver is an instance of positive-influencing COCOMO cost driver. With

respect to the COCOMO, the ideal rating level that has a least impact on effort for cplx is “VL”; hence, its corresponding CoBRA EM should be

zero. CoBRA EM for “cplx” with the rating value of “L” is the difference between COCOMO EM of rating level “L” (0.85) and COCOMO EM of

CoBRA nominal rating level, that is, “VL,” that is, 0.85 � 0.7 = 0.15 (15%). Similar calculations are performed for other EM of each rating level.

In negative-influencing cost drivers, the ideal state of a cost driver with COCOMO is at its largest rating level. As an instance, “acap” is a nega
tive influencing COCOMO cost driver. Its ideal rating level is “VH,” which means if analyst capacities are very high, then the least effort from this

aspect would be imposed on the project. Correspondingly, effort overhead in CoBRA caused by acap is assumed zero (nominal state) when its

value in COCOMO is VH. The next rating level is “H,” and its corresponding CoBRA EM is the difference between its COCOMO EM and

COCOMO EM corresponding to the CoBRA nominal state, that is, “VH,” that is (0.86 � 0.71 = 0.15).

To calculate “sced” EM in CoBRA, the COCOMO rating level that has the lowest EM value is considered as the CoBRA nominal state. The dif
ference between EM of other rating levels of “sced” with N—that is its rating level corresponds to the CoBRA nominal state—constitutes the basis

for calculating the CoBRA EM of other rating levels. The mapping of COCOMO to CoBRA EMs for all effort drivers in each defined rating level is

presented in Table 5.

The pseudo-code of the proposed algorithm for converting collected projects' data in COCOMO (and COCOMO-II) format into their CoBRA

correspondence is shown in Table 6. Using this algorithm, the values of the COCOMO cost drivers of each project collected with the linguistic

words can be replaced with the corresponding CoBRA EMs.

The proposed conversion method can also be applied on COCOMO-II format datasets. The proposed mapping algorithm does not incorporate

the value of COCOMO-II scale factors to the CoBRA EM. There is no such concept as scale factor in CoBRA. We only consider the

17 COCOMO-II cost drivers as CoBRA effort drivers and transform their EMs to CoBRA EMs. Therefore, algorithm 1 would be used for conver
ting the COCOMO-II format data to CoBRA format data. By applying the proposed conversion method on the COCOMO-II dataset, there will be

17 cost drivers whose EMs are shown in Table 4.

4.3 | Determining nominal productivity

In this section, we describe our proposed method for building the CoBRA nominal productivity model from a COCOMO dataset. We utilize

median approach introduced in Ruhe et al. [18] for calculating the nominal productivity (P Nom ), whereas K similar historical projects are identified.

In order to retrieve similar historical projects, we use Euclidean similarity (ES) and Manhattan similarity (MS). [59] ES is defined as

5 | EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN

5.1 | Datasets

To evaluate the proposed method, we test it on both COCOMO and COCOMO-II datasets. Used datasets that are demonstrated in Table 8 are

widely used in previous studies. [1,5,10,50]

COCOMO81 dataset is the original dataset used by Boehm to calibrate COCOMO [8] and has 15 cost drivers. This dataset includes

63 instances of software projects [60] with their cost drivers, size, mode, category of application (type), and effort—we refer to this dataset as

“ ”
COC81. This dataset was later translated to the COCOMO-II format and is available in the SEACRAFT repository. [61] We refer to this

dataset as “COC81-dem.”

“COCOMONASA2” dataset contains 93 projects’ data from different centers of NASA company. COCOMO and COCOMO-II format of this

dataset are respectively available in PROMISE [62] and SEACRAFT [61] repositories. In this paper, we refer to these datasets as NASA93 and

NASA93-dem, respectively.

COCOMONASA dataset contains 60 projects' data in COCOMO format from different centers of NASA from the 1980s to 1990s. It is avail
able in the PROMISE repository. [63] In the rest of the paper, we refer to this dataset as “NASA60.”

“NASA10” dataset is another dataset in COCOMO-II that has 17 instances of software projects. This dataset is presented in Menzies et al. [10]

5.2 | Performance metrics

There are several performance metrics commonly used in SDEE based on absolute residual (AR) and magnitude of relative error (MRE). AR shows

the absolute difference between the actual effort (Y i ) and the estimated effort (Y [b] i ) of the project i:

AR i ¼ jð Y i Þ� Y [b] i j ð9Þ
� �

Mean absolute residual (MAR) is calculated as


P Ni¼1 [j] ð [ Y] [i] Þ� �Y [b] i �j


MAR ¼


, ð10Þ
N


where N denotes the number of instances.

MRE is computed as


MRE i ¼


jð Y i Þ� Y [b] i j
� � ð11Þ

Y i


MMRE specifies the mean magnitude of relative error, and MdMRE is the median of all MREs. Because MMRE can be highly affected by

outliers, [23] MdMRE metric is used in some studies. [23,33,44,64] Despite being criticized by some researcher as being biased toward underestimated

prediction, [50,65] MRE is a popular accuracy statistics that is used in many studies. [1,5,44,50]

Another common and popular metric is PRED(L). [13,23,44] It depicts the percentage of estimates that are within the L percent of the actual value

and is defined as

PRED Lð Þ ¼ [A] ð12Þ
N

where N represents the number of instances and A is the number of projects with MRE less than or equal to L. Commonly, L = 0.25 is considered.

It is desirable for estimation methods to maximize PRED and minimize MAR, MRE, MMRE, and MdMRE. MMRE is sensitive to outliers, and a sin
gle large MRE can skew the MMRE [66] ; hence, it is not a reliable performance metric. Instead, PRED (0.25) is more preferred. [23]

Recently, an unbiased measure introduced by Shepperd and MacDonell [65] called standard accuracy (SA) is used by researchers. [1,5,50] SA for

prediction method P i is defined as

SA ¼ 1 � [MAR] [P] [i] ð13Þ
MAR P 0

where MAR P i is the mean absolute residual for P i and MAR P 0 is the mean of a large number of random guessing runs (1000 in our case). SA shows

how much P i is better than random guessing. Values under zero indicate that performance of the prediction model P i is worse than random

guessing. The values near zero mean that the prediction model is useless. The closer SA values to 1, the better P i .

Idri et al. have shown [67] that PRED(L) is less biased toward underestimates. Moreover, they have shown that SA and PRED(L) measure differ
ent aspects of the method's performance.

|FEIZPOUR ET AL.|13 of 32|
|---|---|
|||


5.3 | Implementation

In order to determine the performance of our proposed method and compare it with others, we used the leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV)

method in our method and other methods. In the LOOCV method, iteratively one of the instances is selected as the test set and the remaining

instances are used as the training set. So, test project is not seen in the training phase.

FIGURE 3 The training phase of the proposed method to determine the optimum number of similar projects (K) and the best similarity

function.

|14 of 32|FEIZPOUR ET AL.|
|---|---|
|||


In order to find the optimal value of k—that depicts the number of similar historical projects—and the similarity function used in the productivity

model of CoBRA, a dynamic search is applied in the training phase. Different combinations of k and two similarity functions are considered to determine

the best k and the best similarity function that minimizes (MdMRE � PRED (0.25)). [44] Therefore, the lower bound for the difference between these two

metrics is “�1.” It is desirable the difference between these metrics be closer to �1. Figure 3 depicts the training phase of the proposed method for

determining the optimum number of similar projects (K) and the best similarity function. Project effort is then estimated as shown in Figure 4.

Few other methods including CART, SVR, K nearest neighborhood (KNN), and random forest (RF) [1,10,23,33,44,50,64,68] are used in SDEE. We

have implemented these methods with Matlab 2017 library with the default settings and compared their perfomance with our proposed method.

We have also compared the proposed method with COCOMO and COCOMO-II by using the default values of the parameters of these models to

demonstrate the performance of the proposed method when calibration of COCOMO is not possible.

6 | RESULTS

In this section, experimental results obtained in each dataset are represented separately. The results obtained in our experiment (MMRE, PRED

(0.25), MdMRE, MAR, and SA) are shown in Tables 9–14. In addition to implementing several well-known and efficient effort estimation methods,

we compared our results with the results reported in the previous studies that have used the same datasets and the same performance metrics.

The results of the conducted experiments on each dataset are also depicted with boxplot and bar charts. Note that, for PRED (0.25) and SA

values, larger are better and for MMRE, MdMRE, and MAR values, smaller are better.

6.1 | Results on COC81 dataset

Table 9 shows the results obtained on COC81. In the most of the previous studies, MMRE and PRED (0.25) are used as performance measures

but the state-of-the-art model [50] has used MAR. Considering the MAR measure, our proposed method has obtained a much lower MAR than in

Jose Thiago and Oliveira [50] (i.e., 290.44 vs. 888).

FIGURE 4 Testing phase.

|FEIZPOUR ET AL.|15 of 32|
|---|---|
|||


On this dataset, COCOMO has obtained better results than our proposed method and other studies with the lowest MMRE, MdMRE,

and MAR value and the highest PRED (0.25) and SA value. This can be explained due to the fact that the COCOMO model is already built

and calibrated on this dataset. This means that COCOMO is perfectly fitted into this dataset. After COCOMO, on this dataset, our pro
posed method has obtained better results than the other methods in all measures, with lower MMRE, MdMRE, and MAR and higher SA

and PRED (0.25).

Figure 5 depicts the distribution of ARs obtained from the estimation methods on the COC81 dataset. COCOMO and our proposed method

have shorter interquartile range in comparison with the other methods, 92.26 and 114.96, respectively.

Figure 6 visually compares the results of the implemented methods with three unbiased metrics. In the case of PRED (0.25) and SA, higher

values and, in the case of MdMRE, lower values are better.

6.5 | Results on NASA60 dataset

NASA60 dataset includes 60 projects in COCOMO format. Results obtained from our proposed method and other existing methods on this

dataset are presented in Table 13. The lowest values of MMRE, MdMRE, and MAR and also the highest values of PRED (0.25) and SA are

achieved by our proposed method. Figure 13 shows the obtained results.

A number of studies have proposed methods to calibrate the coefficients of COCOMO on this dataset. [11,12,16] However, our proposed

method has provided better results without the need of calibration. Moreover, with the proposed method MdMRE and MMRE are 0.15 and 0.25,

respectively. Although previous studies [12,15,16] have obtained lower MMRE, their PRED (0.25) is less than ours. Considering the MAR measure,

our proposed method has resulted in a much lower value than in Jose Thiago and Oliveira. [50] Moreover, the obtained MdMRE by our method is

better than the others.

best results in all measures than the other methods. Figure 15 shows this superiority of the proposed method in SA, MdMRE, and PRED (0.25).

Furthermore, Figure 16 shows that our proposed method has achieved the lowest median, lower quartile (Q1), and upper quartile (Q3) of ARs in

the boxplot chart.

This dataset is rarely used in the previous studies. Xia et al. [1] have proposed a method that uses sequential model-based optimization to find

MdMRE, respectively. Although their SA is greater than ours, MdMREs are equal. Furthermore, their method could not perform well on

COC81-dem and NASA93-dem datasets—see Tables 10 and 12.

6.7 | Statistical analysis

To support the findings about MRE and AR obtained in different experiments, we have conducted Wilcoxon signed ranks test at the significance

level of 0.05. [33,44] This test is used to compare significant differences between average of two dependent samples. In effect, the reported results

show the significant difference between MMRE and MAR of the proposed method and others. Moreover, we have calculated A12 effect size,

which measures the percentage of cases in which other methods have led to higher or equal MRE (AR) compared with the proposed method. [69]

A12 over 0.56, 0.64, and 0.71 respectively indicates small, medium, and large difference.

7 | DISCUSSION

In this section, we provide our discussions and interpretations of the results presented in the previous section.

7.1 | Answers to the research questions

In this section, we answer the research questions based on experiments.

� RQ1: Considering the similarity of the nature of the COCOMO and CoBRA, is it possible (how) to provide a method to generate CoBRA
required data from the datasets collected for COCOMO?

In Section 4, we have proposed a mapping algorithm—Algorithm 1—that converts COCOMO-style dataset to a dataset that is applicable in

CoBRA.

� RQ2: How is the effectiveness of the CoBRA method compared with other effort estimation methods?

Comparison of the proposed method with COCOMO, CART, KNN3, KNN1, SVR, and RF on all six datasets are depicted in Figures 17 and 18. In

these figures, horizontal axis represents the datasets: 1, COC81 dataset; 2, COC81-dem dataset; 3, NASA93 dataset; 4, NASA93-dem; 5, NASA60

dataset; 6, NASA10 dataset.

Figures 17A and 17B respectively compare the MMRE and MdMRE obtained by the methods. It can be seen that MMREs and

MdMREs obtained by the proposed method are lower than other methods on NASA93, NASA93-dem, NASA60, and NASA10 datasets.

However, MMREs and MdMREs of COCOMO on COC81 and COC81-dem are lower than ours. As can be seen in Figure 17C, the MAR

obtained by the proposed method is lower than all other methods on all the datasets, except for the COC81 dataset on which COCOMO

has had the lowest MAR. Results of Table 15 also shows statistically significant difference in MAR and MMRE between our proposed

method and others on different datasets.

FIGURE 18 Comparisons of PREDs and SAs among the proposed model and others.

|FEIZPOUR ET AL.|27 of 32|
|---|---|
|||


Figure 18 compares the PREDs and SAs obtained from the proposed method with other methods in all six datasets. Figure 18A shows that

except on COC81 and COC81-dem, the PREDs (0.25) obtained by the proposed method are higher than all other methods and on all other

datasets. Only COCOMO has had higher PRED (0.25) than the proposed method on COC81 and COC81-dem. As can be seen in Figure 18B, the

SA obtained by the proposed method has been higher than all other methods on all datasets, except on COC81. Only COCOMO on COC81

dataset shows higher SA than the proposed method.

As can be seen in Figures 17 and 18, the performance of the proposed method has been better on the COCOMO-II versions of the

datasets. It seems that CoBRA on COCOMO-II features can better estimate the effort on COCOMO features. Of course, this observation

needs further investigation. Moreover, it can be seen that the proposed method has had better performance than other methods on all

datasets except on COC81. Only COCOMO has shown better performance on COC81, which is not unexpected because COCOMO is cali
brated on this dataset.

� RQ3: At least with how many historical projects CoBRA can predict the software effort accurately?

We have also studied the optimum number of similar projects (k) that are used by CoBRA on the datasets—Figure 19. As is evident from

Figure 19A—except in three cases—10 historical projects are used to estimate projects' effort in CoC81 dataset. However, for estimating the

efforts of projects in COC81-dem, different values of k are used that range from 3 to 10—Figure 19B. Figures 19C and 19D respectively show

that on NASA93—except in one case—and on NASA93-dem dataset—except in thirteen cases—five historical projects are used to estimate the

effort of the projects. The maximum values of k in NASA93 and NASA93-dem are 9 and 7, respectively. Figure 19E shows that in most cases, four

historical projects are used to estimate the projects' effort. However, the maximum value of k in this dataset is 9. Figure 19F shows that in

NASA10, two historical projects are used to estimate projects' effort, except in two cases.

FIGURE 19 The number of historical projects (K) used by proposed method to estimate effort of projects on datasets.

|28 of 32|FEIZPOUR ET AL.|
|---|---|
|||


The experiments show different values of k in different datasets, but with CoBRA, at least two similar historical projects need to estimate

software efforts.

� RQ4: Can CoBRA be a good alternative for COCOMO when there is insufficient historical data to calibrate COCOMO?

As the results of statistical analysis in Table 15 and the results of Table 9–14 show, except the COC81 that COCOMO calibrated on them, our

proposed method can better or the same estimates than the COCOMO.

7.2 | Summary of achievements

The obtained results by our proposed method on six datasets in the COCOMO and COCOMO-II format demonstrate its effectiveness on (1) con
verting COCOMO's data to meet the CoBRA requirement data and (2) superiority of using the proposed method for SDEE over a significant num
ber of existing methods.

Based on the above-discussed findings, we can argue that using the proposed method, more accurate effort estimation of the software pro
jects would be achieved with fewer number of historical projects. Hence, data related to historical projects can be collected in COCOMO

(or COCOMO-II) format that is well-established in the community. Despite the COCOMO method that needs at least 10 historical projects to

have acceptable performance, [5] better estimations would be achieved by applying CoBRA on a reasonably fewer number of transformed historical

projects. As such, the proposed method can be useful and efficient for newly established software companies that do not have much historical

data to estimate software development efforts. Compared with COCOMO, our proposed method has the advantage of not needing any calibra
tion as is required for the parameters of COCOMO. Also, the scarce expertise required to directly collect data for CoBRA is eliminated.

8 | THREATS TO VALIDITY

All experiment-based studies are threatened by a number of issues that must be considered to avoid wrong conclusion.

8.1 | Internal validity

Internal validity examines the question of whether different results can be achieved with regard to different runs or different parameter setups. In

this study, all the estimates were produced using the LOOCV technique in which iteratively a project is selected as the test set and the remaining

projects are used for training; therefore, the test project is an unseen project in training phase, and any bias in the conclusion is avoided. LOOCV

produces the same results on a specific dataset if the experiments are repeated. [67] Furthermore, all parameters and similarity measure in this study

are well defined. The value of k, which specifies k similar historical projects to the target project, is determined using the LOOCV technique in a

dynamic search; therefore, in each run, the same value is obtained for each target project.

8.2 | External validity

External validity is discussed as how the proposed models can be generalized in the real world. COCOMO is still used in SDEE, and calibrating its

coefficients is still a hot topic. [5,11,12,16] Menzies et al. [10] strongly recommend using COCOMO for predicting software effort when COCOMO style

attributes are available.

Our proposed method is based on the fact that when there is no enough local data to calibrate COCOMO parameters, COCOMO cannot be able

to produce accurate estimates. It is unlikely to have access to enough quality historical data in new contexts or in newly established organizations to

calibrate COCOMO. In this case, our proposed method can mitigate this problem. We have tested our proposed method on six well-known and pub
lic datasets in COCOMO and COCOMO-II formats. The datasets contain projects in various contexts such as banking, aerospace, military, and soft
ware. The projects cover a wide range of application domains including management of information system, operating systems, simulation, and signal

processing. Considering the variety of datasets used, it is reasonable to conclude that the proposed method can be effective in the real world.

The other concern of external validity is whether the findings of this study are relevant to the present software development methods. Xia

et al. [1] have argued that despite the popularity of agile methods in software development, waterfall model for developing projects is still in use,

especially in large government and military software contracts. For instance, COCOMO-II is recently used for estimating software development

effort in real aeronautical safety-critical software development project under the DO-178C processes. [70]

|FEIZPOUR ET AL.|29 of 32|
|---|---|
|||


8.3 | Construct validity

Construct validity examines the question of whether a study measures what it really intends to measure. The aim of this study was to investigate

whether the proposed CoBRA is an efficient method for software effort estimation. Although some performance metrics used in this study such

as MMRE and MdMRE have been criticized by some researchers as it is biased toward error underestimations, we have also used two state-of
the-art measures, namely, SA and MAR, to avoid the biasing in the results. Use of these metrics makes the results comparable with a wide range

of prior studies. Furthermore, the use of Wilcoxon signed ranks test on MRE and AR and also A 12 effect size between each pair of the proposed

method and the other comparing methods can minimize the possible threat to construct validity. In addition, a boxplot of ARs is utilized to show

the distribution of error in results and ease the comparison of results. We believe the results and the findings of this study are of the highest

reliability.

9 | CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

Software project managers require accurate development effort estimation to implement, schedule and control software projects successfully. A

number of methods are proposed for software effort estimation. Data-driven methods usually require large sets of historical projects. COCOMO

is a popular parametric data-driven model that is used in waterfall software development process. It has shown good accuracy in the effort predic
tions if its parameters are accurately calibrated on local historical data. These data are usually scarce in software companies, and their collection is

time-consuming and costly. CoBRA as a hybrid method that uses expert knowledge and past completed project data for effort estimation does

not require large dataset and provides accurate estimates of effort. However, collecting CoBRA-required data is complex and costly. In this paper,

we propose a method that extracts CoBRA-required data from COCOMO data and then estimates the development effort of projects using the

CoBRA method. More precisely, we have proposed (1) a mapping algorithm for converting COCOMO EMs to CoBRA EMs and (2) a method for

determining CoBRA productivity model to be extracted from COCOMO's data. With the proposed method, more accurate effort estimates can

be obtained when there is not enough data to calibrate the parameters of COCOMO.

We applied our method on six public datasets and compared the obtained results with a number of well-known methods and also other previ
ous research that have used the same datasets and the performance metrics. The evaluation results showed the proposed method outperformed

a significant number of previous studies and has increased the accuracy of estimates.

It is notable to mention that applying our proposed transforming method has resulted in six public datasets that are applicable in CoBRA.

CoBRA as one of the capable hybrid methods is almost overlooked in the realm of SDEE, and to the best of the authors' knowledge, no public

dataset is released for it. The results of this research can motivate researchers to focus more on the CoBRA method and direct their research to

this forgotten method that can be a beginning for the improvement of this method.
